hero.title: Nick Galante
hero.subtitle: I'm a senior software engineer and technical lead at Charter Communications. I like to work on ambitious technical problems. Over my career, I've architected, implemented, deployed, and maintained technical solutions that have served millions of users at scale. I enjoy working on distributed systems. I have worked extensively improving and scaling microfrontends and enterprise React architectures. I am meticulous and obsessive about performance and optimization. More recently, I've been interested in cryptography, and large language model agentic developer tooling.
hero.cta: Check out some of my projects

Lots of fun.

selectedWork.title: Selected Work
selectedWork.introduction: These are some projects that I felt were worth cherry-picking and noting specifically. If you'd like to learn more about any of these projects, drop me a note!

projects.name: AI / LLM Registry
projects.context: Charter Communications · Principal architect, primary implementer, technical lead maintainer
projects.claim: A company-wide registry for versioned agent assets, built on the durable ideas behind npm and container registries.
projects.description: I architected, implemented, and delivered a vendor-neutral platform for distributing serializable large language model asset configurations (Agents, Skills, Model Configs, MCP Support, etc.) across harnesses and IDEs (Cross Agent/IDE Support). Namespaced assets have owners, semantic versions, dependencies, tags, update and yank semantics, and complete local history. A CAC-based npm client exposes installation, discovery, submission, rollback, and a suite of roughly thirty other operations that support improved agentic development workflows.
evidence: Several hundred to low-thousands of cataloged assets
Adopted company wide across 40 to 50 organizational namespaces
SQLite-backed client history, dependency installation, rollback, and nightly releases
projects.technologies: TypeScript, Bun, npm, CAC, SQLite, Rust, PostgreSQL

projects.name: Springfield
projects.context: Charter Communications · Principal architect, implementer, long-term owner
projects.claim: A deterministic software-intelligence platform that turns a massive system (65+) of distributed frontends into a queryable model of the system.
projects.description: I built Springfield end to end as a stateless ETL system. It clones source packages into deterministic temporary filesystem locations, crawls them in parallel, converts source into ASTs, and runs purpose-built pipelines over the result. Those pipelines map cross-package imports and exports, catalog React components and hooks, reproduce component rendering, and trace downstream service and payload usage. The resulting data lakes are available through REST, GraphQL, MCP tools, and a conversational interface. Models can consume Springfield's facts. This has supported enhanced observability into the system, and worked to starkly increase developer and product velocity.
evidence: 295 total crawled packages and more than 30,000 source files
More than 2,500 modules and 2,500 React components
Complete refresh in under four minutes with zero inference tokens (concurrent automomous ETL pipelines)
Roughly 90,000 database writes in about 875 milliseconds
projects.technologies: TypeScript, Rust, AST analysis, parallel ETL, relational data, GraphQL, REST, MCP

projects.name: Amazon Platform Engineering
projects.claim: Platform work spanning design systems, microfrontends, regulated payments, and production reliability.
projects.description: I founded and technically led Gotham, a design system used across Prime Gaming, Prime Video, and digital-goods experiences. I also proposed, implemented, and owned the migration of a massive monolithic digital goods frontend toward distributed team level microfrontends, enabling autonomous releases, reducing builds from upwards of eleven minutes to under 2 minutes. I solutioned and implemented a microservice and edge function  for European payment and compliance requirements, and built high-availability synthetic monitoring (canaries) for critical customer paths.
evidence: Shared interface foundations across multiple Amazon product organizations
Build time reduced from eleven minutes to six
Payment and compliance orchestration for European markets
Synthetic monitoring for high-availability customer experiences
projects.technologies: React, TypeScript, design systems, microfrontends, AWS, distributed workflows

projects.name: Evergreen Terrace
projects.claim: A private scalable model for gastown that doesn't incinerate tokens.
projects.description: I think everyone takes a swing at one of these in 2026: a persistent queue, specialist agents, shared context, orchestration, and an operational dashboard. Evergreen treats agents as parts of an engineering system rather than a chat window, with explicit ownership and enough persistence and state to resume meaningful work instead of repeatedly rediscovering it.
evidence: Persistent work and context across specialist agents
Operational dashboard and orchestration surfaces
Designed as an inspectable engineering system, not a prompt collection
projects.technologies: TypeScript, Bun, React, agent orchestration, MCP, SQLite

projects.name: Cross-session Context Store
projects.claim: Shared, durable engineering memory for Claude Code, Codex, and Kiro sessions.
projects.description: This one's pretty straight forward. If you've ever used AWS AgentCore Memory this is a private, open source, cross harness compatible version. Its just how you want memory in a harness to work: hands off, loaded on demand, and nothing leaves your machine.
evidence: FTS5 and BM25 retrieval over typed, scoped memories
Review queues, conflict handling, decay, and explicit handoffs
Seventy-five automated tests across the working v0.1
projects.technologies: Bun, TypeScript, SQLite, FTS5, React, MCP

projects.name: Bit Context Protocol
projects.claim: A compact binary format for structured model context.
projects.description: This one's heavily based on some work I had done previously around ext4 filesystems. It's an approach to efficient context window delegation through a dumb byte container protocol medium. It's still in early workings, but the stable prerelease is available for use today.
evidence: RFC and reference implementation
Fuzz testing around binary encoding and decoding
Early workloads measured roughly 30-50% better token efficiency
projects.technologies: Binary protocols, TypeScript, schema design, fuzz testing, LLM context

projects.name: Bundt
projects.claim: A set of independently versioned developer tools built around Bun.
projects.description: Bundt is a system of bun developer tooling. This is to say, developer tooling, built with the same foundational bun toolchain and with a turborepo monorepo approach. Think oxc but with one ten millionth the funding.
evidence: Independent application and library release boundaries
Agent orchestration, documentation, SSR, and local-inference tooling
A practical proving ground for shared packages without forced coupling
projects.technologies: Bun, TypeScript, React, SSR, MCP, monorepo tooling

projects.name: DeckVault
projects.claim: A deliberately over-engineered Pokémon platform for exploring systems architecture with a domain I actually enjoy.
projects.description: Deckvault is a pokemon-themed love letter to microservice infrastructures, frameworkless performant server rendered react, and passion projects, and maybe, just maybe, a tool for Pokemon trainers to build better decks.
evidence: React server rendering across a service-oriented backend
Relational, graph, and embedded persistence used for distinct jobs
A long-running architecture laboratory with real product constraints
projects.technologies: React 19, Bun, Rust, GraphQL, PostgreSQL, Neo4j, SQLite, Docker

principles.title: How I Engineer
principles.introduction: These are some principles that I've come to value over my career, in regards to how we approach software as engineers:

items.title: Ownership
items.description: Ownership involves a model of what I'd call perpetual accountability. Software is not done when it ships, and it's not even really done when it's sunsetted. When something goes down, at 3 AM for a critical service, you very likely want someone answering the pager with the mentality that this is their responsibility to fix, and that itself stems from a model of ownership.

items.title: Bias for Action
items.description: This comes down to being able to, in your software ecosystem, correctly identify one way and two way doors. Engineers who sprint through two way doors responsibly

items.title: Strong Opinions, Loosely Held
items.description: This one's simple. Have opinions. Ground them in data, benchmarks, tangible evidence. Be able to support them and demonstrate why they are correct for this problem. Drop them when someone else's strong opinion is better suited for the problem based on the data they brought to the table. When we all operate this, we all improve each other.

items.title: Measure before claiming
items.description: If you aren't able to ground what you are saying in data, there's a great likelihood there's something better you could be saying.

items.title: Prefer deterministic systems before inference
items.description: I use models where ambiguity requires them. If a parser, protocol, query, or state machine can produce the fact, I would rather make the fact reproducible. Prefer reproducible deterministic systems, always. Use model inference where needed. Fairly simple.

items.title: Abstractions justify their cost
items.description: An abstraction should remove a recurring burden or enforce a valuable constraint. A small simple system is almost inarguably the desired state of all software systems, it's just not the pragmatic state of some.

items.title: Operational quality is architecture
items.description: Accessibility, performance, observability, reversibility, and release behavior belong in the roadmap from day one, and never thought of as a fast follow.

items.title: Follow the problem across boundaries
items.description: Useful systems rarely respect frontend, backend, infrastructure, or native labels. Become an expert at problem solving and at the craft of software, and solve problems wherever they hide.

elsewhere.title: Elsewhere
paragraphs: Away from a keyboard, I am usually with my fiancée and our dogs, accumulating Pokémon knowledge, or enduring the Dallas Cowboys with the sort of loyalty that should probably be studied.

I read avidly about pen-and-paper ciphers, modern encryption, and the long evolution between them. Cryptography is an intellectual interest, not a production credential I am trying to smuggle into a skills matrix.
I also like the Eagles. The band. This clarification has become operationally necessary.

closing.title: I like using software to solve problems, try out new ideas, and improve our lives
closing.description: If you have an idea for a project and are looking for support, I'm usually very happy to offer assistance through consulting or direct collaboration.
